2.text: assistant, and then leave him the herd. A childless man, feeling that his end

3.text: is approaching, sometimes even calls in a kinsman or a friend, who lives

4.text: alone, and hands over his property to him. More frequently such a childless

5.text: man will adopt some boy or girl, also from one of his kin, have him or her

6.text: married, and then he makes him the principal heir of the house and the herd.

7.text: It sometimes happens that a rich reindeer-breeder leaves his herd without any

8.text: definite heir. This may occur, for instance, because of some disease which

9.text: has taken away the only son and heir. The old father, from mere sorrow,

10.text: may follow soon after, since the Chukchee are “soft to die.”¹ In such cases,

11.text: the kinsmen come; and by counting the degrees of kinship decide who is the

12.text: nearest to the deceased. There exist, however, no settled rules about this

13.text: matter. I was told that in earlier times the family-group, would gather and

14.text: come to a decision, but of late no such gatherings are known to me. Kinsmen

15.text: of the same degree may divide the inheritance into equal shares, or the poorer

16.text: man will receive a larger share. On the other hand, I know of cases where

17.text: those of the kinsmen who were at hand took the whole, and the other rel-

18.text: atives, though nearer to the deceased, could get nothing. Thus, for instance,

19.text: while I was on the Wolverene River, a quarrel took place about such an

20.text: inheritance. An old Chukchee of Maritime extraction, who had a good-sized

21.text: herd, died heirless. His herd was taken by a third cousin (parent’s cousin’s

22.text: child), who came with him from their parental village, and now was the front-

23.text: house master of the neighboring camp. Nobody protested, and a few years

24.text: passed away without incident. The man who received the inheritance died

25.text: also, and the herd passed to his son, Akɪmlɵˊkê. Then two young men came

26.text: from the Arctic shore, who said that they were sons of a first-cousin of the

27.text: deceased: so they had a better right to the property than Akɪmlɵˊkê. They

28.text: requested restitution. Akɪmlɵˊkê was a “strong man” (eˊrmečɪn), always ready

29.text: for strife: so he refused to comply with the request. The younger of the two

30.text: brothers, however, whose name was Uˊmkɪ (“polar bear”), was a large fellow

31.text: of considerable strength and temper. He declared that he would rather die

32.text: than go back empty-handed. While I was there, they met at a large reindeer-

33.text: course, and nearly came to blows, but were prevented by the others present.

34.text: I left the country before the matter came to a final issue.

35.text: When the principal heir is a daughter, who stays in the father’s

36.text: house, even after she is married, her rights to the inheritance are the same

37.text: as those of a male heir. A daughter who is married elsewhere receives only

38.text: the animals marked with her private ear-mark. Some of these remain in her

39.text: father’s herd, even after her marriage. On the division of the inheritance,

40.text: they fall to her possession, anyway. A female relation of more remote degree

41.text: has no part in the inheritance of a childless man, and cannot contend with
